summary: BBN's host status report for December 6 to 18, 1971, with excluded hosts and a table of daily test results. It was replaced by RFC 288.

eli5.summary: A report on which network computers were up during two weeks in December.

subtitle: Network host status report for December 6 to 18, 1971

tldr.problem: ARPANET operators continued tracking host availability to monitor network health and identify non-functioning systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 287 reports daily test results from the BBN Terminal IMP for two weeks in December, showing the status of each host and listing those currently excluded from testing.
tldr.outcome: This became a routine operational report, with the practice continuing through many subsequent RFCs. It was replaced by RFC 288.

today: RFC 287 is historic and replaced by RFC 288. It documents the ARPANET's operational status in December 1971, showing the network was still in active development and testing with frequent changes in host availability and configurations.

sections.title: Status Report
sections.content:
RFC 287 is a status report from BBN dated December 22, 1971, covering December 6 to 18. The report notes that the BBN prototype Terminal IMP (Network Address 158) was unavailable for most of the previous two weeks due to hardware debugging, so there was no host status report for November 22 to December 6.

Several hosts are excluded from daily testing, falling into two categories: those not expected to function as servers for at least two weeks, and those intended as user-only hosts or supporting network operations only.
sections.eli5: This is another report showing which computers worked that week. Some computers are skipped because they are not supposed to be servers or they are broken.

sections.title: Excluded Hosts
sections.content:
Category 1: Hosts not expected to function as servers for at least two weeks

  • BBN PDP-10 (B) at Network Address 133
  • RAND PDP-10 at Network Address 71
  • CASE PDP-10 at Network Address 13
  • AMES ILLIAC and B6500 at Network Address 15
  • AMES IBM-360/67 at Network Address 16

Category 2: User-only hosts and network operations hosts

This category includes Terminal IMPs (at AMES, MITRE, NBS, and BBN) used only for testing, the Network Control Center Computer (Network Address 5) used solely for statistics gathering, and specific user-only hosts such as the RAND IBM-360/65, HARVARD PDP-1, ILLINOIS PDP-11, and NBS PDP-11.

The NBS Terminal IMP (Network Address 147) was installed in Washington at the beginning of December.
sections.eli5: Some computers were broken or not ready to test. Some were just for sending information out, not for receiving requests. This list shows which ones to skip.

sections.title: Host Status Results
sections.content:
The report provides two weeks of daily test results across two pages, with status codes for each host each day. The codes are the same as in previous reports: D (dead), H (half-open), O (open), R (refused), and T (timed out).

A summary table shows each host's current status or predicted service status. For example, UCLA's SIGMA-7 is listed as a server, the UCLA IBM-360/91 offers Remote Job Service, SRI's PDP-10 is server status, MIT Multics is a server, and Stanford's PDP-10 is predicted to be a server soon.
sections.eli5: The report shows if each computer was dead, open, timed out, refused, or half-open. Some hosts were supposed to become servers in the future.
